title: Convergence and Compactness I: the Sequential Tychonoff and Arzelá-Ascoli
html:
Following the Terry's notes (up to some reorganising and exercise solving), I aim to develop the sequential Tychonoff theorem, which says an at most countable product of sequential compact spaces is again sequential compact. This has a beautiful application - the Arzelá-Ascoli theorem, giving characterisation of precompact subsets in the space of bounded continuous functions, which is particular useful in PDEs (and part of the reason to write this up). Along the way I also included (also from Terry's notes) an interesting and insightful concept - that of an ultrafilter.

From introductory mathematical analysis one is familiar with sequences, which in the simplest case is a countable infinite tuple a0,a1,… {a_{0},a_{1},\dots}a0​,a1​,… of reals, and which is said to converge to a limit a∈R {a\in\mathbb{R}}a∈R if for every ϵ>0 {\epsilon>0}ϵ>0, there exists N∈N {N\in\mathbb{N}}N∈N such that

∣an−a∣≤ϵ\displaystyle |a_{n}-a|\leq\epsilon∣an​−a∣≤ϵ

for all n≥N {n\geq N}n≥N. The number a {a}a captures the approximate position (in the sense of absolute value) of the sequence (an)n∈N {(a_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}}(an​)n∈N​ when n {n}n is large enough. The concept of convergence of elements in a metric space (X,d) {(X,d)}(X,d), such as L1 {L^{1}}L1-convergence, goes along the same line. To say it in another fashion, a sequence (fn)n {(f_{n})_{n}}(fn​)n​ is said to converge to f∈X {f\in X}f∈X if for any open metric ball around f {f}f, the tail of the sequence is eventually (that is, after discarding some first finite number of terms) contained in it. Note that as a conseqeunce of the non-degenercy of the metric d {d}d, the limit, if exist, is unique. One can also consider more generally, the convergence in a topological space (X,F) {(X,\mathcal{F})}(X,F), where (xn)n {(x_{n})_{n}}(xn​)n​ is said to converge to x∈X {x\in X}x∈X if for any neighborhood U {U}U of x {x}x, the tail of the sequence is eventually contained in U {U}U. This convergence of sequences in a topological space X {X}X can also be seen as a continuous property of a mapping from N∪{+∞} {\mathbb{N}\cup\{+\infty\}}N∪{+∞} to X {X}X. More precisely, the mapping is given by

x(⋅):n↦xn;+∞↦x.\displaystyle x(\cdot):n\mapsto x_{n};+\infty\mapsto x.x(⋅):n↦xn​;+∞↦x.

Here we give N {\mathbb{N}}N its natural ordering ≥ {\geq}≥ and declare +∞≥n {+\infty\geq n}+∞≥n for all n∈N {n\in\mathbb{N}}n∈N. It follows then N∪{+∞} {\mathbb{N}\cup\{+\infty\}}N∪{+∞} is a well-ordered set. The order topology on N∪{+∞} {\mathbb{N}\cup\{+\infty\}}N∪{+∞} is defined by declaring singletons {n} {\{n\}}{n} for each n∈N {n\in\mathbb{N}}n∈N and sets of the form [n,+∞]:={m∈N∪{+∞}:m≥n} {[n,+\infty]:=\{m\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{+\infty\}:m\geq n\}}[n,+∞]:={m∈N∪{+∞}:m≥n} to form a base of the topology. The map x(⋅) {x(\cdot)}x(⋅) is then continuous. The convergence in a topological space can be characterised by the follwing ``subsequence principle'', which is useful for identifying convergence that are not topologisable.

Proposition 1 (Urysohn's subsequence principle) Let (xn)n∈N {(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}}(xn​)n∈N​ be a sequence of in a topological space X {X}X, and x∈X {x\in X}x∈X. The following are equivalent:

*- xn→x {x_{n}\rightarrow x}xn​→x as n→∞ {n\rightarrow\infty}n→∞;

  • Every subsequence of xn {x_{n}}xn​ converges to x {x}x;
  • Every subsequence has a further subsequence that converges to x {x}x.*

Proof: The only part not clear is (3)⇒(1) {(3)\Rightarrow(1)}(3)⇒(1). Suppose (xnj)j {(x_{n_{j}})_{j}}(xnj​​)j​ has a further subseqeunce converging to x∈X {x\in X}x∈X but xn {x_{n}}xn​ does not. Then xn {x_{n}}xn​ has a subsequence does not converge to x {x}x, which in turn has no further subseqeunce converging to x {x}x, a contradiction. □ \Box□

Example 1 Pointwise almost everywhere convergence is not a convergence defined through topology. Indeed, consider the space L∞[0,1] {L^{\infty}[0,1]}L∞[0,1] and the ``typewriter seqeunce''

fn,k(x)=χ[k−12n,k2n]\displaystyle f_{n,k}(x)=\chi_{[\frac{k-1}{2^{n}},\frac{k}{2^{n}}]}fn,k​(x)=χ[2nk−1​,2nk​]​

where k=1,…,2n {k=1,\dots,2^{n}}k=1,…,2n. fn,k {f_{n,k}}fn,k​ converges to zero in L∞ {L^{\infty}}L∞-norm, so if fn,k {f_{n,k}}fn,k​ were to converge pointwisely a.e., the limit should be zero. But each point x∈[0,1] {x\in[0,1]}x∈[0,1] belongs to some dydic interval of length 2−n {2^{-n}}2−n, for each n {n}n. We see that fn,k {f_{n,k}}fn,k​ does not converge to zero pointwisely a.e. Yet it is clear that every subsequence has a further subsequence converging to zero pointwisely a.e., because of L∞ {L^{\infty}}L∞ convergence.

1.1. Interaction with the properties of the topological space

We begin by asking when the limit defined in the sense above, if exists, is unique. By an almost tautological argument, the uniqueness will follow from the Hausdorff property of the topological space. It is also easy to create artificial examples:

Example 2 Consider a set with two points X={a,b} {X=\{a,b\}}X={a,b}, with the topology F={X,∅,{a}} {\mathcal{F}=\{X,\emptyset,\{a\}\}}F={X,∅,{a}}. By design we see that a {a}a and b {b}b cannot be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods, and hence (X,F) {(X,\mathcal{F})}(X,F) is not Hausdorff. Then the constant sequence (xn:=a)n {(x_{n}:=a)_{n}}(xn​:=a)n​ converges to b {b}b also.

Roughly speaking, the Hausdorff property infers that the topology contains enough open sets in order to be able to distinguish distinct points by disjoint open sets.
A more interesting question is when we have convergence, at least at the subsequence level. It is perhaps well known that

Theorem 2 (Bolzano-Weierstrass) A bounded sequence in R {\mathbb{R}}R has a convergent subsequence.

Proof: There is a subsequence converging to the sup⁡{an} {\sup\{a_{n}\}}sup{an​}. Alternatively, one constructs a monotone subsequence, then by monotone convergence theorem concludes that the subsequence converges. □ \Box□

In particular, any sequence in a bounded subset E⊂R {E\subset\mathbb{R}}E⊂R contains a converging subsequence. Such E {E}E is said to be sequential precompact. If the limit always belongs to the set E {E}E, it is then said to be sequential compact. For metric spaces, sequential compactness has a rather complete characterisation:

Theorem 3 (Heine-Borel) Let (X,d) {(X,d)}(X,d) be a metric space. The following are equivalent:

*- X {X}X is sequential compact;

  • X {X}X is compact, i.e. every open cover has a finite subcover;
  • Any collection of closed sets with finite intersection property (FIP) has non-empty intersection: if (Fα)α∈A {(F_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in A}}(Fα​)α∈A​ a collection of closed subsets of X {X}X is such that any finite subcollection has non-empty intersection, then the entire collection has non-empty intersection;
  • X is complete, and totally bounded, i.e. for each ϵ>0 {\epsilon>0}ϵ>0 there is a finite number of metric balls of radius ϵ {\epsilon}ϵ covers X {X}X.*

First we can show (2)⇔(3) {(2)\Leftrightarrow(3)}(2)⇔(3), which holds regardless X {X}X is a metric space or not. Taking complement of the open sets in the cover (Gα)α∈A {(G_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in A}}(Gα​)α∈A​, we obtain a collection of closed sets (Fα)α∈A {(F_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in A}}(Fα​)α∈A​. That the cover has a finite subcover means the corresponding finite subcollection of closed sets has empty intersection (de Morgan's law). Taking contrapositive, we obtain (3) {(3)}(3). the other direction is similar.
For (1)⇒(4) {(1)\Rightarrow(4)}(1)⇒(4), to show X {X}X is complete, take (xn) {(x_{n})}(xn​) to be a Cauchy sequence. By sequential compactness, it contains a converging subsequence. Remember the sequence itself is Cauchy, thus the sequence must converge to the same limit. Now suppose X {X}X is not totally bounded. Then there is ϵ0>0 {\epsilon_{0}>0}ϵ0​>0 such that no finite collection of ϵ0 {\epsilon_{0}}ϵ0​-balls can cover X {X}X. Take x1∈X {x_{1}\in X}x1​∈X. Choose xn {x_{n}}xn​ outside of the ϵ0 {\epsilon_{0}}ϵ0​-balls centered at previous x1,…,xn−1 {x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1}}x1​,…,xn−1​. Thus we obtained a sequence

d(xn,xm)≥ϵ0\displaystyle d(x_{n},x_{m})\geq\epsilon_{0}d(xn​,xm​)≥ϵ0​

for all n≠m {n\neq m}n=m. It cannot contain converging subsequence, a contradiction. Now for (2)⇒(1) {(2)\Rightarrow(1)}(2)⇒(1), we need an important property for metric topology.

Definition 4 A topological space (X,F) {(X,\mathcal{F})}(X,F) is called first countable if for each x∈X {x\in X}x∈X, there is a countable family Bx,1,Bx,2,… {B_{x,1},B_{x,2},\dots}Bx,1​,Bx,2​,… of open neighborhood of x {x}x that forms a neighborhood basis of x {x}x, i.e. for any open set Vx {V_{x}}Vx​ containing x {x}x, there is a Bx,j {B_{x,j}}Bx,j​ such that Bx,j⊂Vx {B_{x,j}\subset V_{x}}Bx,j​⊂Vx​.

Lemma 5 A metric space is first countable.

Proof: Take metric balls centered at x {x}x with positive rational radius. □ \Box□

Now for any seqeunce (xn) {(x_{n})}(xn​) in a compact metric space X {X}X, it must accumulate in X {X}X, say at x {x}x. Taking a countable neighborhood of x {x}x and selecting one member of the sequence in each, we get a converging subsequence.
Finally, (4)⇒(3) {(4)\Rightarrow(3)}(4)⇒(3), whose proof is unavoidably more complicated than the previous ones. Let (Fα) {(F_{\alpha})}(Fα​) be as in (3) {(3)}(3). Suppose X {X}X is covered by G1,…,Gn {G_{1},\dots,G_{n}}G1​,…,Gn​. Then at least one of Gi {G_{i}}Gi​ intersects all of Fα {F_{\alpha}}Fα​'s, and call such a covering set rich. Indeed, if not, then each Gi {G_{i}}Gi​ must miss one Fi {F_{i}}Fi​, hence by de Morgan's law the intersection of F1,…,Fn {F_{1},\dots,F_{n}}F1​,…,Fn​ is empty.
Since X {X}X is totally bounded, we can cover X {X}X by a sequence of finite families of metric balls {Bn,1,…,Bn,mn}n {\{B_{n,1},\dots,B_{n,m_{n}}\}_{n}}{Bn,1​,…,Bn,mn​​}n​ with each Bn,j {B_{n,j}}Bn,j​ centered at xn,j {x_{n,j}}xn,j​ of radius 2−n {2^{-n}}2−n. If we look at the centers {xn,j} {\{x_{n,j}\}}{xn,j​}, as an infinite set it accumulates somewhere in X {X}X, say at x {x}x. So there is a seqeunce of balls Bk,jk {B_{k,j_{k}}}Bk,jk​​, each intersect with the next one, with decreasing radius to zero. Then xk {x_{k}}xk​ is a cauchy sequence, and by completeness of X {X}X it converges to x {x}x.
Now observe that the sequence of balls Bk,jk {B_{k,j_{k}}}Bk,jk​​ must eventually all be rich. Then x {x}x is a limit point of every Fα {F_{\alpha}}Fα​. Since each Fα {F_{\alpha}}Fα​ is closed, we have x∈Fα {x\in F_{\alpha}}x∈Fα​ for all α {\alpha}α, and so we are done.
We see that sequential compactness in a metric topology is the same with compactness. These two notions in general, however, are different.
Bearing this in mind, we now discuss more about the Hausdorff property and compactness in a topological space. It turns out that they go in ``opposite directions'':

Proposition 6 Let (X,F) {(X,\mathcal{F})}(X,F) be a topological space.

*- Suppose X {X}X is compact. Then every closed subset is also compact. If we put any weaker topology F′ {\mathcal{F}'}F′ than F {\mathcal{F}}F (i.e. F′⊂F {\mathcal{F}'\subset\mathcal{F}}F′⊂F ) on X {X}X, X {X}X will still be compact. In particular, the trivial topology is always compact.

  • Suppose X {X}X is Hausdorff. Then every compact subset is closed. If we put any stronger topology F′ {\mathcal{F}'}F′ than F {\mathcal{F}}F (i.e. F′⊃F {\mathcal{F}'\supset\mathcal{F}}F′⊃F ) on X {X}X, X {X}X will still be Hausdorff. In particular, the discrete topology is always Hausdorff.
  • If F′⊂F {\mathcal{F}'\subset\mathcal{F}}F′⊂F and F′ {\mathcal{F}'}F′ is a Hausdorff topology and F {\mathcal{F}}F is a compact topology, then F′=F {\mathcal{F}'=\mathcal{F}}F′=F.*

In contrast to the Hausdorff property, compactness is often attained when there are ``fewer'' open sets. This indicates that we will have to put a ``weaker'' topology in order to gain ``more converging subsequences''.
To see (3) {(3)}(3) is true, observe that since F′⊂F {\mathcal{F}'\subset\mathcal{F}}F′⊂F, any closed subset in the Hausdorff topology is also closed in the compact topology, and by (1) {(1)}(1), it is compact in the compact topology. Also because of F′⊂F {\mathcal{F}'\subset\mathcal{F}}F′⊂F , any compact subset in the compact topology is compact in the Hausdorff topology, and by (2), it is closed in the Hausdorff topology. We thus conclude two topology has the same collection of closed sets.
We thus see that on the same set a Hausdorff topology cannot be strictly weaker than a compact topology, so compact Hausdorff topology (abbr.CH) is in some sense special - for example, it is also normal, a property not even shared by the locally compact Hausdorff topology. This particularity can be grasped precisely by the ultrafilters on it.

Definition 7 A filter p {p}p on a set X {X}X is a collection of subsets of X {X}X that is

*- closed under finite intersection;

  • monotone: if E∈p {E\in p}E∈p and E⊂F {E\subset F}E⊂F, then F∈p {F\in p}F∈p;
  • ∅∉p {\emptyset\notin p}∅∈/p.*

A filter p {p}p is said to be an ultrafilter if in addition for any E⊂X {E\subset X}E⊂X, exactly one of E {E}E and X\E {X\backslash E}X\E lies in p {p}p. For x∈X {x\in X}x∈X and an ultrafilter p {p}p, p {p}p is said to converge to x {x}x if every neighorhood of x {x}x belongs to p {p}p.

Lemma 8 Every filter has finite intersection property (FIP). Any collection of sets with FIP is contained in a filter.

Proof: Let E1,…,En {E_{1},\dots,E_{n}}E1​,…,En​ belong to a filter p {p}p. By monotone property, their intersection ∩iEi {\cap_{i}E_{i}}∩i​Ei​ is in p {p}p by closure property by finite intersectioning. By monotone property, it cannot be empty.
Now let E {\mathcal{E}}E be a collection of set with FIP. We join more sets according to the monotone property. Clearly finite intersection property is preserved. Note that ∅ {\emptyset}∅ is not in E {\mathcal{E}}E, nor will be added in during the process. □ \Box□

Lemma 9 (Ultrafilter lemma) Every filter is contained in an ultrafilter

Proof: Ordering the filters via inclusion, Zorn's lemma shows that a filter p {p}p is contained in a maximal filter p~ {\tilde{p}}p~​. By maximality, it is easy to see that X∈p~ {X\in\tilde{p}}X∈p~​. Now suppose there is E⊂X {E\subset X}E⊂X such that both E,X\E∉p~ {E,X\backslash E\notin\tilde{p}}E,X\E∈/p~​. Then any set in p~ {\tilde{p}}p~​ must have non-empty portions in both E,X\E {E,X\backslash E}E,X\E, which is impossible for X {X}X. □ \Box□

Thus in particular any collection of sets with FIP is contained in an ultrafilter.

Proposition 10 Let (X,F) {(X,\mathcal{F})}(X,F) be a topological space.

*- X {X}X is Hausdorff if and only if every ultrafilter on X {X}X has at most one limit.

  • X {X}X is compact if and only if every ultrafilter on X {X}X has at least one limit.*

Thus in particular X {X}X is CH if and only if every ultrafilter on X {X}X has one and only one limit.

Proof: For (1) {(1)}(1), suppose an ultrafilter p {p}p on X {X}X has two limits x {x}x and x′ {x'}x′. Then p {p}p contains every neighborhood of x,x′ {x,x'}x,x′. Since X {X}X is Hausdorff, x,x′ {x,x'}x,x′ can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods if x≠x′ {x\neq x'}x=x′. Hence we must have x=x′ {x=x'}x=x′. For the ``if'' part, if there exist x≠x′ {x\neq x'}x=x′ cannot be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods, then any two neighborhoods of x {x}x and x′ {x'}x′has non-empty intersection, and hence any finite collection of them has FIP. These neighborhoods are thus contained in an ultrafilter by the above lemmas. But then the ultrafilter will have at least two limits,
For (2) {(2)}(2), let p {p}p be an ultrafilter on X {X}X. Recall that in the proof of Heine-Borel we have compactness equivalent to any collection of closed sets with FIP having non-empty intersection. By the above lemmas, it suffices to show p {p}p has the latter property if and only if X {X}X is compact, and is easily verified. □ \Box□

Remark 1 As is probably anticipated, the characterisation of compactness by properties of ultrafilters sheds light on how to fix the discrepancy between sequential compactness and compactness, namely, we can introduce a collection of objects with a more general labelling system (i.e. a directed set) other than the natural numbers, creating the notion of a net. But as I am mainly interested in convergence of sequences and their usage in studying PDEs, and I haven't yet seen nets play a role in that direction, I shall not try to include it here. Nonetheless they are interesting when studying topological spaces themselves.

1.2. From the viewpoint of product spaces, and their sequential compactness property

To make our discussion more precise, we need several definitions.

Definition 11 Let (X,F) {(X,\mathcal{F})}(X,F) be a topological space.

*- A base for the topology is a collection B {\mathcal{B}}B of open sets such that every open set in X {X}X can be expressed as the union of sets in B {\mathcal{B}}B. The elements of B {\mathcal{B}}B are called basic open set.

  • A sub-base for the topology is a collection B {\mathcal{B}}B of subsets of X {X}X such that F {\mathcal{F}}F is the weakest topology that makes B {\mathcal{B}}B open, that is B {\mathcal{B}}B generates F {\mathcal{F}}F, by arbitrary unions and finite intersections. The elements of B {\mathcal{B}}B are called sub-basic open set.*

Familiar examples include metric balls in a metric topology, where they form a base for the metric topology; half-open intervals in R {\mathbb{R}}R, where they form a sub-base for the usual topology on R {\mathbb{R}}R. One can go from a sub-base to a base, much like in case from half-open intervals to any open intervals, by joining their finite intersections. A result (whose proof depends on Zorn's lemma) useful in our discussion is the following, which we shall just assume.

Theorem 12 (Alexander sub-base theorem) (X,F) {(X,\mathcal{F})}(X,F) is a compact topological space if and only if every sub-basic open cover has a finite subcover.

Definition 13 (Product spaces) Given a family (Xα,Fα)α∈A {(X_{\alpha},\mathcal{F}_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in A}}(Xα​,Fα​)α∈A​ of topological spaces, let X:=∏α∈AXα {X:=\prod_{\alpha\in A}X_{\alpha}}X:=∏α∈A​Xα​ be the Cartesian product, equipped with projection maps πα:X→Xα {\pi_{\alpha}:X\rightarrow X_{\alpha}}πα​:X→Xα​. The product topology on X {X}X is defined to be the topology generated by the cylinder sets πα−1(Uα) {\pi_{\alpha}^{-1}(U_{\alpha})}πα−1​(Uα​), where Uα∈Fα {U_{\alpha}\in\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}}Uα​∈Fα​, that is, these cylinder sets form a sub-base. Equivalently, such is the weakest topology that makes the projection maps continuous.

Perhaps surprisinly, pointwise convergence can be formulated as convergence in a product space.

Example 3 Let (X,F) {(X,\mathcal{F})}(X,F) be a topological space and Y {Y}Y a set. We define

XY:={f:Y→X}\displaystyle X^{Y}:=\{f:Y\rightarrow X\}XY:={f:Y→X}

to be the space of all functions form the set Y {Y}Y into the topological space X {X}X. Since at each y∈Y {y\in Y}y∈Y one can assign all possible values in X {X}X, the space can be in fact viewed as a product space

XY=∏y∈YXy\displaystyle X^{Y}=\prod_{y\in Y}X_{y}XY=y∈Y∏​Xy​

where each Xy {X_{y}}Xy​ is a copy of X {X}X labeled by y {y}y. The projection πy:f↦f(y) {\pi_{y}:f\mapsto f(y)}πy​:f↦f(y) is the evaluation map at y∈Y {y\in Y}y∈Y. Then the product topology on XY {X^{Y}}XY is generated by the sets Gy,V={f∈XY:f(y)∈V} {G_{y,V}=\{f\in X^{Y}:f(y)\in V\}}Gy,V​={f∈XY:f(y)∈V} for all y∈Y {y\in Y}y∈Y and all V⊂X {V\subset X}V⊂X open. A sequence of functions fn:Y→X {f_{n}:Y\rightarrow X}fn​:Y→X is said to converge to f:Y→X {f:Y\rightarrow X}f:Y→X pointwisely if for each y∈Y {y\in Y}y∈Y, fn(y)→f(y) {f_{n}(y)\rightarrow f(y)}fn​(y)→f(y) as n→∞ {n\rightarrow\infty}n→∞. Compositing with the projection maps, we see that fn→f {f_{n}\rightarrow f}fn​→f in the product topology if and only if fn→f {f_{n}\rightarrow f}fn​→f pointwisely.

Now we come back to the discussion of sequential compactness. Suppose now we have two sequential compact spaces X1 {X_{1}}X1​ and X2 {X_{2}}X2​, and form their product X1×X2 {X_{1}\times X_{2}}X1​×X2​. Then for any sequence (x(m))m {(x^{(m)})_{m}}(x(m))m​ in the product space, by ignoring the first slot, we can extract a subsequence (x(m1,j))j {(x^{(m_{1,j})})_{j}}(x(m1,j​))j​ whose first slots form a converging sequence in X2 {X_{2}}X2​. Then based on the obtained sequence, by ignoring the second slot, we can extract a further subsequence (x(m2,j))j {(x^{(m_{2,j})})_{j}}(x(m2,j​))j​ whose first slots form a converging sequence in X1 {X_{1}}X1​. Thus we obtain the sequence (x(m2,j))j {(x^{(m_{2,j})})_{j}}(x(m2,j​))j​ convergent in both slots.
When we have a product of at most countably many sequential compact spaces, by the same construction we can obtain a subsequence that is convergent is every slot. Note that if the number is infinite we cannot yet conclude a convergent subsequence in the product space. But we can use the ``diagonalisation trick'': we pick x(mi,i) {x^{(m_{i,i})}}x(mi,i​) as the i {i}i-th member to form a new subsequence, which is convergent by construction. By Example 3, pointwise convergence is the same as convergence in the product space. Thus this argument yields the sequential Tychonoff thoerem, we state it as:

Theorem 14 (Sequential Tychonoff) Any at most countable product of seqeuntially compact topological spaces is sequentially compact.

As an application of the theorem, we now quickly formulate and prove the theorem of Arzelá-Ascoli, which characterises when a subset of BC(X→Y) {BC(X\rightarrow Y)}BC(X→Y) is precompact, under the uniform metric topology.

Definition 15 Let (X,F) {(X,\mathcal{F})}(X,F) be a topological space, (Y,dY) {(Y,d_{Y})}(Y,dY​) be a metric space. Let (fα)α∈A {(f_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in A}}(fα​)α∈A​ be a family of bounded continuous functions BC(X→Y) {BC(X\rightarrow Y)}BC(X→Y).

*- (fα) {(f_{\alpha})}(fα​) is said to be pointwisely bounded if for every x∈X {x\in X}x∈X, the set {fα(x):α∈A} {\{f_{\alpha}(x):\alpha\in A\}}{fα​(x):α∈A} is bounded in Y {Y}Y.

  • (fα) {(f_{\alpha})}(fα​) is said to be pointwisely precompact if for every x∈X {x\in X}x∈X, the set {fα(x):α∈A} {\{f_{\alpha}(x):\alpha\in A\}}{fα​(x):α∈A} is precompact in Y {Y}Y.
  • (fα) {(f_{\alpha})}(fα​) is said to be equicontinuous if for every x∈X {x\in X}x∈X, and for each ϵ>0 {\epsilon>0}ϵ>0, there is a neighborhood U {U}U of x {x}x such that dY(fα(x′).fα(x))≤ϵ {d_{Y}(f_{\alpha}(x').f_{\alpha}(x))\leq\epsilon}dY​(fα​(x′).fα​(x))≤ϵ for all x′∈U {x'\in U}x′∈U and all α∈A {\alpha\in A}α∈A.
  • If (X,dX) {(X,d_{X})}(X,dX​) is also a metric space, the family (fα) {(f_{\alpha})}(fα​) is said to be uniformly equicontinuous if for each ϵ>0 {\epsilon>0}ϵ>0, there is δ>0 {\delta>0}δ>0 such that such that dY(fα(x′).fα(x))≤ϵ {d_{Y}(f_{\alpha}(x').f_{\alpha}(x))\leq\epsilon}dY​(fα​(x′).fα​(x))≤ϵ for all x,x′ {x,x'}x,x′ such that dX(x,x′)≤δ {d_{X}(x,x')\leq\delta}dX​(x,x′)≤δ and all α∈A {\alpha\in A}α∈A.*
